q: What is machine learning?
short: Programming computers to improve at a task from data rather than explicit rules: performance P on task T improves with experience E.
detail: Traditional programming maps data + program → output; ML maps data + outputs → program (a model). Mitchell's ⟨T, P, E⟩ makes a learning task precise.
example: Spam filter: T = classify emails, P = % correct, E = labelled emails.
follow: Give T, P, E for a recommender.
How is ML different from statistics?
mistakes: Defining ML as 'AI that thinks'.

q: How do AI, ML and data science relate?
short: ML is a subset of AI; data science overlaps both and uses ML as one tool for decisions from data.
detail: AI includes search, planning and reasoning beyond learning. Data science spans collection, cleaning, analysis, statistics and domain expertise.
example: A rule-based chess engine is AI but not ML.
mistakes: Treating the three as synonyms.

q: Supervised vs unsupervised vs reinforcement learning?
short: Supervised learns from labelled pairs; unsupervised finds structure without labels; reinforcement learns a policy from delayed rewards.
detail: Supervised → regression/classification; unsupervised → clustering, association, dimensionality reduction; RL → control via trial and error, maximising cumulative reward.
example: Price prediction / customer segmentation / game playing.
mistakes: Calling clustering 'classification'.

q: Classification vs regression?
short: Classification predicts a category; regression predicts a real number.
detail: Both are supervised. Losses differ (cross-entropy/0–1 vs squared error) and so do metrics (accuracy/F1 vs RMSE/R²).
example: Benign vs malignant; sea-ice extent by year.
follow: Is predicting a rating 1–5 classification or regression?
mistakes: Deciding by the model name (logistic 'regression' is a classifier).

q: When should you not use machine learning?
short: When exact rules exist and are cheap to code (payroll), when there's no data, or when errors are unacceptable and unexplainable.
detail: ML adds data dependence, maintenance and uncertainty. Use it when expertise is missing or tacit, rules change, or personalisation is needed.
follow: How do you check whether there is a learnable pattern?
mistakes: Using ML because it is fashionable.

q: What are features and labels?
short: Features are the measured inputs describing an example; the label is the target we want to predict.
detail: employability uses CGPA, communication, aptitude and programming skills as features and 'job offered?' as the label.
example: Used car: brand, year, mileage → price.
mistakes: Including the label (or a proxy of it) among the features.

q: What is semi-supervised learning?
short: Learning from a small labelled set plus a large unlabelled set.
detail: Typical approaches: cluster then label clusters, self-training with confident pseudo-labels, graph label propagation.
example: Photo apps: name a face once, the app finds the rest.
follow: What can go wrong with pseudo-labels?
mistakes: Assuming more unlabelled data always helps.

q: Batch vs online learning?
short: Batch trains on all data at once; online updates the model one example (or small chunk) at a time as data arrives.
detail: Online suits streams, huge datasets (out-of-core) and drifting distributions; batch is simpler and more stable.
follow: How does the learning rate affect online learning?
mistakes: Thinking online learning needs no evaluation.

q: Instance-based vs model-based learning?
short: Instance-based compares new points with stored examples (k-NN); model-based fits parameters and discards the data.
detail: Instance-based has no training cost but slow, memory-heavy prediction; model-based is fast at prediction and compact.
follow: Which handles irregular boundaries more naturally?
mistakes: Saying k-NN has no hyperparameters.

q: Describe the ML workflow.
short: Check ML fits → collect data → preprocess and explore → choose model, loss, regularisation → optimise → tune hyperparameters → evaluate, analyse errors, iterate.
detail: The car-price demo follows it: objective, data gathering, train/test split, EDA, linear regression, objective function, optimisation, test-set evaluation.
follow: Where does deployment and monitoring fit?
mistakes: Tuning on the test set.

q: Explain Mitchell's definition with an example where E is not labelled data.
short: A program learns if performance P on task T improves with experience E; E can be self-play or interaction.
detail: Checkers: T = play checkers, P = % games won, E = games against itself. That's experience without human labels, closer to RL.
follow: What is P for a self-driving car?
mistakes: Assuming E must be a labelled dataset.

q: Why is the ML spam filter easier to maintain than a rule-based one?
short: It learns indicative patterns from data and can be retrained automatically as spam evolves, instead of growing an unmaintainable rule list.
detail: Rules need manual updates after each new trick; learned models adapt when retrained on new labelled mail and often generalise to unseen variants.
example: New spam phrase 'For U' caught without a new rule.
follow: How would you keep the training data fresh?
mistakes: Ignoring adversarial adaptation by spammers.

q: What is generalisation and why do we need a test set?
short: Generalisation is performance on unseen data; a held-out test set estimates it because training error is optimistically biased.
detail: Training minimises empirical risk; the true risk can be much higher if the model overfits. Test data must play no part in training or tuning.
example: 95.6% test accuracy on iris vs 100% on training.
mistakes: Reusing the test set for model selection.

q: What does the interpretability–accuracy trade-off mean?
short: Flexible models (boosting, deep nets) are usually more accurate on complex data but harder to explain than linear models or small trees.
detail: The chart is explicitly opinionated: on many tabular problems simple models are competitive, and post-hoc tools (SHAP, LIME) narrow the gap.
example: Credit scoring often prefers explainable models.
mistakes: Treating the chart as a law.

q: You have 1M customer records and 500 labelled churners. Which learning setup?
short: Supervised with careful handling of imbalance, possibly semi-supervised to exploit unlabelled data.
detail: Check whether the other records are known non-churners (then it's fully labelled but imbalanced) or truly unknown (semi-supervised/PU learning). Use stratified splits and precision/recall metrics.
mistakes: Reporting accuracy on 0.05% positives.

q: How can unsupervised learning have a test phase?
short: A trained clustering can assign new points, e.g. to the nearest centroid, and be evaluated for stability or downstream usefulness.
detail: : assign a new cat/dog image to the cluster with the closer centroid. Evaluation uses internal indices or labels if available (ARI).
mistakes: Assuming clustering outputs are always meaningful.

q: What is a baseline and why start with one?
short: The simplest sensible predictor (constant, majority class, last value). Any model must beat it to be worth deploying.
detail: In the car demo, a constant H0 = 9 has total L1 error 17.27; the best constant (median) 13.17; a line 12.57.
mistakes: Comparing models without a baseline.

q: Hypothesis class vs learning algorithm?
short: The hypothesis class is the set of functions considered (e.g. all lines); the algorithm searches it to pick one using data and a loss.
detail: Choosing the class sets the inductive bias; too small underfits, too large risks overfitting.
mistakes: Blaming the optimiser for a too-simple class.

q: A model is great offline but degrades after deployment. Why?
short: Distribution shift (concept or data drift), leakage in offline evaluation, or training–serving skew.
detail: Monitor input distributions and performance; retrain (online or periodic); audit features for future information.
example: Fraud patterns change after a new payment method.
mistakes: Retraining blindly without diagnosing.

q: What is reinforcement learning's objective?
short: Learn a policy π(a|s) that maximises expected cumulative (discounted) reward.
detail: The agent observes, acts, receives reward, updates the policy and iterates. Exploration vs exploitation is central.
example: Robot avoiding fire in the example.
follow: What is the discount factor for?
mistakes: Calling RL supervised because rewards look like labels.

q: Define empirical risk minimisation and its pitfalls.
short: Choose h minimising average training loss; pitfalls are overfitting, optimistic error estimates and sensitivity to label noise.
detail: $\hat h=\arg\min_h\frac1n\sum\ell(h(x_i),y_i)$. Control capacity with regularisation, validation and more data; bounds relate true and empirical risk via capacity (VC dimension, Rademacher complexity).
mistakes: Equating low training loss with learning.

q: What is the no-free-lunch theorem's practical message?
short: No algorithm is best for all problems; assumptions (inductive bias) must match the data.
detail: Averaged over all possible target functions, all learners perform equally. Practical ML works because real problems have structure.
example: Trees win on tabular data, CNNs on images.
follow: How do you choose an algorithm then?
mistakes: Searching for a universally best model.

q: What is the i.i.d. assumption and when does it fail?
short: Training and test examples are independent draws from the same distribution; it fails with time series, grouped data and drift.
detail: Violations make random splits leak information. Use time-based or group splits and monitor drift.
mistakes: Random K-fold on temporal data.

q: How would you formalise semi-supervised learning assumptions?
short: Cluster, smoothness and manifold assumptions: points close in dense regions share labels.
detail: Without such assumptions unlabelled data cannot help. Methods: entropy minimisation, consistency regularisation, label propagation.
mistakes: Ignoring class-imbalanced pseudo-labels.

q: Online learning vs mini-batch SGD?
short: Both update incrementally; online processes a stream once and adapts to drift, mini-batch SGD loops over a fixed dataset for many epochs.
detail: Online learning is analysed with regret bounds; SGD with convergence to an empirical minimum.
mistakes: Assuming online learners converge to a fixed model under drift.

q: Design T, P and E for a network anomaly detector.
short: T: flag anomalous KPI windows; P: precision/recall at an alert budget; E: historical KPIs, mostly unlabelled plus a few incident labels.
detail: Likely unsupervised or semi-supervised; evaluate on labelled incidents, tune for the operations team's alert capacity.
mistakes: Using accuracy on rare anomalies.

q: What is data leakage?
short: Information unavailable at prediction time sneaks into training features or preprocessing.
detail: Examples: target-derived features, scaling fitted on all data, future timestamps. Leads to great offline and poor live results.
example: Using 'account closed date' to predict churn.
mistakes: Fitting preprocessors before splitting.

q: Is k-NN parametric?
short: No: its complexity grows with the data; it stores instances rather than a fixed number of parameters.
detail: Non-parametric methods adapt to any boundary given enough data but suffer from the curse of dimensionality.
follow: What is the curse of dimensionality?
mistakes: Equating 'non-parametric' with 'no hyperparameters'.

q: How do you evaluate clustering without labels?
short: Internal indices (silhouette, Davies–Bouldin), stability under resampling, and usefulness for a downstream task.
detail: Silhouette compares within-cluster cohesion to nearest-cluster separation; stability checks consistency across bootstraps.
example: Customer segments evaluated by campaign lift.
follow: Why can silhouette mislead for non-convex clusters?
mistakes: Picking k by eye only.

q: Why is median the best constant under L1 loss and mean under L2?
short: The derivative of Σ|y−c| is the count imbalance around c (zero at the median); the derivative of Σ(y−c)² is zero at the mean.
detail: Car data: any c in [2.51, 6.95] gives total L1 13.17; the mean 5.42 minimises squared error.
follow: Which loss is more robust to outliers?
mistakes: Using the mean as the L1-optimal constant.
